title: LangGraph — Audio Guide

chapters.title: Mental Model
chapters.script:
You may wonder what problem LangGraph solves. The naive linear approach — prompt, then large language model, then output — fails for real-world AI applications. Simple chains cannot handle loops, conditional branching, multi-agent coordination, or persistent state across turns. Consider a customer support bot that must remember conversation history across multiple turns, decide whether to escalate to a human agent, execute tools like checking order status or processing refunds, loop back to gather more information if the initial query is ambiguous, and support parallel execution for fetching data from multiple sources simultaneously. These requirements demand an execution model where state is first-class, control flow is dynamic, and persistence is built in. LangGraph provides exactly this: a graph-based execution model where each node reads from and writes to a shared state object, edges can be conditional, and the entire execution can be paused, resumed, and replayed.

Picture a whiteboard where each step of a process writes its results, and the next step reads what it needs. The whiteboard persists between steps — if a step fails, you can see what was written and resume from there. Arrows on the whiteboard show which step comes next, but some arrows have conditions: if the answer is good, go to end; otherwise, go back to research. Multiple people can write to the same whiteboard simultaneously, and a supervisor watches the whiteboard and decides who works next.

Here is a minimal agent in about fifteen lines. You define a state schema as a typed dictionary with fields for messages and next action. You define a node that calls the large language model and returns an update with the response and the next action. You define a conditional edge function that inspects the state and returns either tool or final. You add nodes for model and tool, create a conditional edge from model to either tool or END, a normal edge from tool back to model, and an edge from START to model. When you invoke the compiled graph with a message, it loops until a final answer is produced. This is a complete, stateful agent loop that demonstrates the core ideas of state, nodes, and conditional edges.

chapters.title: Core Concepts
chapters.script:
State is the heart of every LangGraph application. It is a typed dictionary or Pydantic model that holds all data flowing through the graph. Key properties include immutable snapshots, meaning each node receives a read-only view; reducer functions for merging updates from multiple nodes; and thread isolation, where each conversation gets its own state namespace. The state acts as a central hub that all nodes read from and write to. Reducers define how updates to the same key are merged when multiple nodes write in parallel. For example, you can use operator dot add to append to a list of messages, or write a custom reducer to merge dictionaries with updates taking priority.

Nodes are Python functions, synchronous or asynchronous, that take the current state and return a dictionary of updates. They can be large language model calls, tool executors, human approval steps, conditional logic, or API calls. For instance, a node might call an LLM with the current conversation history, execute a tool call from the last message, or pause for human approval before sensitive actions.

Edges define control flow between nodes. Normal edges are unconditional transitions from one node to the next. Conditional edges are functions that inspect the state and return the name of the next node. For example, you can route to a billing agent if the query contains billing, or to tech support if it contains technical, or to a general agent otherwise.

Checkpointing saves state after every node execution, enabling fault tolerance, human-in-the-loop, and time travel. You have several checkpointers: MemorySaver for development and testing, where state stays in memory only; SqliteSaver for single-server production, using a local SQLite file; and PostgresSaver for multi-server production, backed by a PostgreSQL database. Each thread identifier creates an independent conversation with its own state namespace, so you can run many conversations simultaneously without interference.

The Command object allows a node to set the next node and update state in one step. This is essential for agent loops where the large language model decides the next action. For instance, if the LLM makes a tool call, you return a Command with goto set to tool executor and an update containing the response. If it produces a final answer, you return a Command with goto set to END.

chapters.title: How It Works
chapters.script:
The graph lifecycle has five stages. First, definition: you create a StateGraph with a state schema, then add nodes and edges. Second, compilation: you compile the graph with a checkpointer to create a CompiledGraph. Third, invocation: you call graph dot invoke with an input dictionary and a config that includes a thread identifier. Fourth, execution loop: the runtime loads the state for that thread, executes the current node, applies the updates returned by the node, saves a checkpoint, and routes to the next node based on edges. Fifth, termination: the graph routes to the special END node or hits the recursion limit you set.

Consider a simple question-answering agent. You define a state with fields for query, context, answer, and needs retry. The retrieve node does a similarity search on a vector store and returns context. The generate node uses the context and query to produce an answer from an LLM, setting needs retry to true if the answer contains the phrase I don't know. The check quality edge function returns either retry or done based on the needs retry flag. If retry, the retry node expands the search with a different query generated by the LLM and loops back to generate. When you invoke the graph with a query, it retrieves, generates, checks quality, and either returns the answer or retries.

For real-time applications, LangGraph supports multiple streaming modes. You can stream the full state after each node, stream only the state updates from each node, or stream individual tokens from large language model calls. Each mode serves different needs, from debugging to live user interfaces.

The NodeInterrupt mechanism pauses execution and waits for external input. For example, before executing a sensitive action like sending an email or deleting data, you raise a NodeInterrupt with a description of the pending action. In a frontend, a human can review and approve or reject. You then resume by calling app dot update state with the approved action, and the graph continues from the interrupted node.

chapters.title: Runtime Internals
chapters.script:
LangGraph's runtime is inspired by Google's Pregel system for large-scale graph processing. Execution proceeds in supersteps, which are rounds of parallel computation. In each superstep, all nodes that have incoming edges from the previous superstep execute in parallel. Nodes receive messages, which are state updates from the previous superstep, process them, and send messages to the next superstep. This bulk synchronous parallel model enables deterministic, parallel execution with bounded memory.

State keys are implemented as channels that buffer updates. When multiple nodes write to the same channel in one superstep, the reducer merges them. Different channel types handle different merge patterns. LastValueChannel keeps only the most recent value and is the default for simple fields. AppendChannel accumulates values in a list, which is what you get when you use operator dot add as a reducer. Custom channels allow you to define your own merge logic for complex data structures.

Because state is checkpointed after every superstep, any execution can be replayed exactly. The checkpointer stores the thread identifier, the step number, and a full state snapshot. To replay, you load the state at step N and re-execute nodes from step N plus one. This capability is critical for debugging, testing, and auditing production systems.

Each thread identifier gets its own state namespace in the checkpointer. Threads are completely isolated — no state leaks from one conversation to another. This enables multi-tenancy: one graph can serve many users simultaneously without interference.

LangGraph is fully asynchronous. Nodes can be defined as async functions, and the runtime uses asyncio dot gather to run nodes in parallel within a superstep. Checkpointer writes can be batched for performance in high-throughput scenarios.

chapters.title: Patterns
chapters.script:
One common pattern is the supervisor agent. A supervisor large language model decides which sub-agent to call next. The state includes a next agent field and a shared messages list. Structured output using Pydantic ensures deterministic routing. The supervisor node inspects the conversation and returns a Command with goto set to the chosen agent, or to END if the work is done.

Another pattern is parallel tool execution using a map-reduce approach. You use the Send API to fan out to multiple identical tool nodes in parallel. A planner node returns a list of Send objects, each targeting a fetch URL node with different parameters. Each fetch URL node fetches one URL and writes its result into a dictionary keyed by index. Then an aggregator node combines all fetched content into a single string.

For sensitive actions, you add human-in-the-loop by interrupting before dangerous tool calls such as send email, execute SQL, or delete data. You compile the graph with interrupt before a list of node names. The frontend shows the proposed action, a human approves or rejects, and you call app dot update state to resume with the approved action.

To handle long-running conversations, you use persistent memory with summarization. You employ PostgresSaver for long-term persistence and add a summarization node that fires when the messages list exceeds a threshold. The summarization node asks the LLM to summarize older messages and keeps only the most recent ones, preventing context window overflow.

For safety, you add guardrails with pre and post processing. A validate input node checks for policy violations like personally identifiable information before allowing the LLM to respond. If a violation is found, it routes to a reject node. After the LLM responds, a validate output node checks for harmful content. If harmful content is detected, it routes to a rephrase node, which then loops back to validation until a clean response is produced.

chapters.title: Common Pitfalls
chapters.script:
One of the most common mistakes is state mutation without reducers. If two nodes write to the same state key without a reducer, the second write overwrites the first. Always define reducers for list and dictionary fields. Use the annotated type with operator dot add to ensure that multiple writes are appended correctly.

Infinite loops in the agent executor can occur when the large language model keeps calling tools without producing a final answer. Set a recursion limit when compiling the graph, for example twenty-five steps. Also add a node that checks the iteration count and forces a final answer after a maximum number of turns, say ten.

Checkpointer bottlenecks are another pitfall. Using MemorySaver in production means state is lost when the server restarts. Use PostgresSaver for durability. To reduce latency, batch checkpoint writes and use asynchronous execution.

As your graph grows, you can end up with an overly complex topology — fifty or more nodes with a hundred or more edges. This becomes spaghetti and hard to debug. Encapsulate complex workflows into subgraphs, which you can add as a single node in the parent graph.

Ignoring token limits in shared state is dangerous. The messages list grows unboundedly, eventually causing context overflow and LLM truncation or failure. Implement a trimming or summarization node to keep the state within your token budget.

Finally, conditional edge functions that raise exceptions on unexpected state values will cause the graph to fail with an obscure error. Add a try-catch block in your edge function and return a safe default router, such as a general agent, when the routing logic crashes.
